newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says gaps wide in tense Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: PLO says gaps wide in tense Hebron talks.

text.p: An Israeli handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron appeared more elusive on Wednesday than before when Palestinian officials called negotiations "extremely tense" and the gaps "still very wide".

U.S. mediator Dennis Ross failed in five hours of talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to close a deal on the town of 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews, already delayed for 10 months because of security concerns and other issues.
"The gaps are still very wide," Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters. He said the sides were wrangling over peace moves to follow Hebron.

An aide to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that Israel wanted to put off until 1999 the last of three handovers of rural West Bank lands that under a 1995 interim peace deal were due to be completed by September 1997.
"The last redeployment is a very, very contentious issue. Our interpretations are very far apart," said the aide, Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan.

PLO officials blasted the Israeli proposal, saying it violated timetables set under the 1995 peace deal it signed with the Israeli government which Netanyahu ousted in May on a promise to take a harder line in peace talks.

"The meeting upstairs is extremely tense because the statements that were made today destroyed all hopes that we could reach an agreement," Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani told reporters during Ross's meeting with Arafat.
Abu Rdainah said the Palestinians still wanted U.S. guarantees that Israel would implement the agreement.

Israeli peace negotiator Dan Shomron told Israel Radio on Wednesday that despite the hardships on future deadlines, "I am sure also that a way will be found for a compromise that will bring about also an agreement in the matter of Hebron".
But Nabil Amr, an adviser to Arafat on negotiations, said a crisis had emerged.
"This is a result of the dangerous attempt by Netanyahu to merge the interim phase and the 'final-status' stages which we cannot accept," he told Reuters.

Agreement on the thornier "final-status" issues -- the future of Jerusalem, the fate of Jewish settlers and Palestinian refugees and the question of statehood for Palestinians -- is also due in 1999 under peace deals already signed.
"The problem is also that the Americans, although they are trying hard, are allowing the Israeli internal crisis direct the talks instead of having the agreement be the basis," Amr said.

Some in Netanyahu's largely right-wing and religious cabinet have opposed the deal outright, fearing for the safety of the Jewish settlers there and viewing the town, the burial place of the biblical Abraham, as the birthright of the Jews.
